prompt: The city column had 28 distinct values, and 25 once trimmed. How many spellings existed only because of whitespace at the ends?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: Why does the lesson print the São Paulo spellings with `ascii()`?
hint: What does the screen hide?

choices.text: It removes the accents before printing
choices.why: It shows them as escapes, which is the opposite of removing them.

choices.text: It writes invisible characters as escapes
choices.why: Right: the trailing space shows inside the quotes, and the combining tilde as `\u0303`.

choices.text: It sorts the values the way PostgreSQL would
choices.why: `sorted` did the sorting; `ascii` only changes how each value is written.

choices.text: It converts the text to Latin-1 so it fits the terminal
choices.why: The terminal handles UTF-8; nothing was converted.

prompt: Why does the collapse step replace `\s+` instead of two literal spaces?
hint: Not every blank character is the space bar.

choices.text: It also catches tabs, line breaks and odd spaces
choices.why: Right, and `+` takes any run of them at once.

choices.text: Literal spaces cannot appear in a regular expression
choices.why: They can; they just match only the ordinary space.

choices.text: `\s+` also removes accents
choices.why: It touches whitespace only.

choices.text: It is faster on long columns
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; coverage is.

prompt: Which function is meant for building a key that will be compared?
hint: Think of `Straße`.

choices.text: `title()`
choices.why: That writes `Da Silva` and `Mcdonald`; it is for display, and badly.

choices.text: `upper()`
choices.why: It works for most text but is not the function designed for comparison.

choices.text: `strip()`
choices.why: That trims spaces; case is untouched.

choices.text: `casefold()`
choices.why: Right: it folds `ß` to `ss`, which `lower()` leaves alone.

prompt: Why does the cleaning keep the original name beside the key instead of lower-casing the name itself?
hint: Who reads which column?

choices.text: Lower-cased names take more space in the database
choices.why: They take the same space.

choices.text: pandas cannot lower-case a column in place
choices.why: It can; the reason is the reader.

choices.text: Keys compare; names are shown to people
choices.why: Right. A lower-cased name would go out on the next invoice.

choices.text: Keys must never contain capital letters by law
choices.why: No law is involved.

prompt: What does `'DA SILVA'.title()` return?
hint: It capitalises each word.

choices.text: `'Da Silva'`
choices.why: Right, where Portuguese writes `da Silva`.

choices.text: `'da Silva'`
choices.why: That would need a rule about particles, which `title()` lacks.

choices.text: `'DA SILVA'`
choices.why: `title()` changes the case.

choices.text: `'da silva'`
choices.why: That is `lower()`.

prompt: `'São'` in NFC is 3 characters long. How long is it in NFD?
hint: The tilde becomes its own character.

prompt: Why is normalising every text column to NFC safe to do on the way in?
hint: What does a reader see change?

choices.text: It removes every accent, which keys need anyway
choices.why: NFC keeps the accents, composed.

choices.text: It converts the text from UTF-8 to Latin-1
choices.why: It stays UTF-8; only the form of the characters changes.

choices.text: It turns `²` into `2` and `ﬁ` into `fi` everywhere
choices.why: That is NFKC, which loses information and is meant for keys.

choices.text: It changes nothing visible
choices.why: Right, and it makes equal what should be equal.

prompt: Which of Quitanda Verde's systems sent names and cities in NFD?
hint: Lesson 1 found 213 São Paulos that looked like the others.

choices.text: The website
choices.why: The website writes NFC.

choices.text: The shops' till
choices.why: The till writes Latin-1, a different matter.

choices.text: The app
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The 2023 migration
choices.why: That produced mojibake.

prompt: Removing accents makes `país` and `pais` the same key. Why is that acceptable for a city key and not for stored text?
hint: The key is for the machine.

choices.text: Keys merge spellings; stored text must stay right
choices.why: Right. Merging two spellings of one name costs less than splitting it.

choices.text: Cities never have accents
choices.why: São Paulo does.

choices.text: Stored text is kept in NFD while keys are kept in NFC
choices.why: Both are stored in NFC here.

choices.text: Removing accents is irreversible only for keys
choices.why: It is irreversible for both; that is why stored text keeps them.

prompt: In PostgreSQL, the extension that removes accents is called ___.
hint: It is named after what it does.

prompt: How did `São Paulo` become `SÃ£o Paulo`?
hint: `ã` is two bytes in UTF-8.

choices.text: Somebody typed it on a keyboard set to another language
choices.why: No keyboard produces `Ã£` for `ã`; it is a decoding error.

choices.text: Its UTF-8 bytes were read as Latin-1
choices.why: Right: `0xC3` became `Ã` and `0xA3` became `£`.

choices.text: The app wrote it in NFD
choices.why: NFD looks identical on screen; this does not.

choices.text: The CSV export added a pound sign as a separator
choices.why: The separator is the comma.

prompt: Put the repair of a mangled value in order.
hint: Run the mistake backwards.
items: Check the value carries the signature `Ã`
Encode the text as Latin-1 to get the original bytes
trap: Skipping the check breaks clean text: `São` as Latin-1 is not valid UTF-8.

prompt: What happens if the mojibake repair runs on a clean `São`?
hint: `ã` in Latin-1 is a single byte.

choices.text: Nothing: clean text passes through unchanged
choices.why: `0xE3` alone is not valid UTF-8.

choices.text: It becomes `SÃ£o`, the original damage
choices.why: That is the original damage, made the other way round.

choices.text: It is converted to NFD
choices.why: Encodings and normal forms are different things.

choices.text: It fails, or loses the letter
choices.why: Right; that is why the repair is applied only where `Ã` appears.

prompt: How many customers' names carry the 2023 migration's damage?
hint: The count printed above the three examples.

prompt: Why does the last step from eleven spellings to five cities need a list somebody wrote?
hint: What does `bh` mean?

choices.text: Fuzzy matching is not available in pandas
choices.why: RapidFuzz works with pandas, and `bh` is nothing like `belo horizonte` anyway.

choices.text: The remaining spellings are all typos
choices.why: `bh` and `rj` are deliberate abbreviations.

choices.text: No rule knows that `bh` is Belo Horizonte
choices.why: Right: what is left is knowledge, not mechanics.

choices.text: Lists are faster than functions
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

prompt: Next month a customer types `Sampa`. What should the mapping step do, and why?
hint: A spelling not in the list should be visible.

choices.text: Keep `sampa` as a sixth city in the report
choices.why: That is the defect the list exists to prevent.

choices.text: Leave it blank, so the gap gets counted
choices.why: Right. Then somebody adds `sampa` to the list on purpose.

choices.text: Assign it to the most common city
choices.why: Right this time by luck, and wrong for the next unknown spelling.

choices.text: Drop the customer from the file
choices.why: The customer exists; only the spelling is unknown.

prompt: Match each step to its PostgreSQL function.
hint: The table in the last section.

prompt: Why is the SQL mojibake repair applied only to rows with `Ã`?
hint: What does Latin-1 not hold?

choices.text: Latin-1 cannot hold every character
choices.why: Right, and clean rows do not need it anyway.

choices.text: `unaccent` must run before it
choices.why: Order matters, but not that way: the repair comes before removing accents.

choices.text: PostgreSQL limits functions to ten rows
choices.why: There is no such limit.

choices.text: Only those rows are in UTF-8
choices.why: Every row is UTF-8; these hold the wrong characters in it.

prompt: Put the general steps of the cascade in order.
hint: Repair before you fold.
trap: Removing accents before the repair turns `Ã£` into `A£`, which no longer encodes back to the original bytes.

prompt: A colleague proposes replacing every customer name with its plain key to "clean the file". What is wrong with that?
hint: The key is for the machine.

choices.text: Keys are slower to compare
choices.why: They are faster, if anything.

choices.text: Plain keys cannot be stored in CSV
choices.why: They are ordinary text.

choices.text: Nothing; plain keys are the cleaned names
choices.why: `joao` on an invoice to João is not clean.

choices.text: It loses accents and capitals
choices.why: Right: keep the name, add the key.
